claims.claim: Documentation is the written or electronic record of a patient's care — the assessments, medications, treatments, education, and responses that are recorded in the patient's chart. The ANA describes documentation as the record nurses create of their services, used by the care team, payors, and the legal system.
Accurate documentation ensures continuity of care: it gives subsequent caregivers a comprehensive understanding of the patient's history, current condition, and the care already received.
Documentation is a communication tool within the health care team: it keeps all members aware of the patient's current status and recent changes, even those without direct contact with the patient.

The patient record is a legal record: documentation serves medical and legal purposes, documentation of medication administration is part of the patient's legal medical record and may be used if legal action is initiated, and incomplete, inaccurate, or untimely documentation can impede legal fact-finding.

The saying 'if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done' reflects nursing's documentation culture: because the chart is the durable record used by the care team, payors, and the legal system, the written entry is treated as the evidence of the care provided.

The ANA's principles require high-quality documentation to be accessible, accurate, relevant, clear, concise, complete, legible, thoughtful, and timely (contemporaneous), and each entry must be authenticated, dated, and time-stamped by its author, with nothing added or inserted later.
Timeliness: charting in real time is necessary for maintaining accurate and up-to-date patient records.
Completeness: entries should describe care specifically — what was done and how the patient responded — rather than vague summaries such as 'wound care performed'.
Objectivity: documentation should record the care provided and the patient's response — the facts — not opinions, judgments, or interpersonal conflicts.

Chart types: the admission record is the initial record upon admission (medical history, medications, allergies, reason for admission); progress (narrative) notes give a detailed account of the patient's condition, care, and response; the medication administration record (MAR) tracks the drug, dose, route, time administered, who administered it, and who ordered it; the discharge record summarizes the stay so the next care setting continues informed.

An electronic health record (EHR) is a digital version of the patient's paper chart: a real-time, patient-centered record that makes information available instantly, brings together medical history, diagnoses, medications, allergies, and test results, and can be created and consulted by authorized providers across more than one health care organization.

Corrections: a mistaken paper entry is corrected by drawing a single line through the error, adding the date and your initials, and recording the correct entry — never by erasing, covering, or obscuring the original; electronic entries are corrected within the system.

Documentation is sometimes viewed as burdensome or as a distraction from patient care, yet high-quality documentation is a necessary and integral part of nursing practice — the care story that outlives the shift.

conflictingEvidence.issue: 'If it wasn't documented, it wasn't done' read as a literal statement of fact.
positions: The saying is widespread in nursing education and practice, and it captures that the record is the durable evidence of care, used by the team, payors, regulators, and the legal system.
Care can occur without being charted, so the saying is best read as a professional expectation and risk-management rule rather than a literal claim that undocumented care never happens.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the saying factually as part of nursing's documentation culture and anchors it to the record's verified functions (continuity, communication, legal evidence) without claiming undocumented care never occurs.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How a charting error is corrected depends on the format of the record.
positions: Paper: draw a single line through the error with the date and initials; never erase, use multiple lines, or cover the entry (OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills 11.3).
Electronic records are corrected inside the system, typically through an edit function that preserves an audit trail.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the paper rule in full and notes briefly that electronic entries are corrected within the system.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft described documentation only as 'a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations' with no clinical content — no definition tied to patient records, no principles, and no record types.
The draft's framing of documentation as a study aid ('a label on a toolbox drawer') had no connection to patient care records and was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate draft with a source-verified lesson: a working definition of documentation as the written record of a patient's care, the three purposes (continuity, communication, legal record), the four principles (accurate, timely, complete, objective) with original examples, the named chart types and the EHR, the avoidance list (opinions, vague words, erasing corrections), and the honest framing.
rightsIssues: OpenStax books carry an explicit notice that the books may not be used to train or be ingested into large language models without OpenStax's permission — recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY with aiIngestionAllowed false; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.
The ANA pamphlet 'Principles for Nursing Documentation' (2010) is © American Nurses Association, all rights reserved — recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Fundamentals of Nursing, Section 14.5: Guidelines for Effective Documentation (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (per this subject's source-map). openstax.org serves the section HTML; also read via Wayback Machine capture 2025 of the canonical URL. Book published September 4, 2024. Supports: the ANA's six principles for nursing documentation (characteristics: accessibility, completeness, legibility, timeliness; education; policies; protection systems; authenticated dated entries; standardized terminology); the wide range of documented data (vital signs, medication administration, assessments, responses); purposes — continuity of care, communication within the health care team, a clear and objective record, risk management, medical and legal purposes; charting in real time; complete descriptions ('wound care performed' vs. a detailed entry); charting care, not conflicts (facts, not disagreements); source-oriented documentation table (admission sheet — initial record upon admission with medical history, medications, allergies, reason for admission; narrative note — detailed account of condition, care, and response); SOAP/PIE/focused-charting methods. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Clinical Nursing Skills, Section 11.3: Documentation of Medication Administration (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (per this subject's source-map). Read live 2026-08-22 (book published June 26, 2024). Supports: documentation of medication administration as part of the patient's legal medical record that may be used if legal action is initiated; the medication administration record (MAR) as the record tracking the medications administered, dose, route, time, instructions, who administered, and who ordered; the correction rule — a mistaken paper entry is noted by drawing a single line through the error with the date and initials, using only one line, never multiple lines, squiggly lines, Wite-Out, or erasing; electronic entries corrected within the system; approved-abbreviation rules to prevent medication errors. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What Are Electronic Health Records (EHRs)? (HealthIT.gov FAQ)
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. healthit.gov serves a script-rendered FAQ; read via Wayback Machine capture (id_ form) of the canonical URL. Supports: EHRs are, at their simplest, digital (computerized) versions of patients' paper charts; EHRs are real-time, patient-centered records that make information available instantly and bring together in one place everything about a patient's health — medical history, diagnoses, medications, immunization dates, allergies, radiology images, and lab and test results; a key feature is that an EHR can be created, managed, and consulted by authorized providers and staff across more than one health care organization. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

Supports: clear, accurate, and accessible documentation as an essential element of safe, quality, evidence-based nursing practice; documentation as the record nurses create of their services for use by payors, the legal system, government agencies, and accrediting bodies; communication within the health care team (accurate, timely, contemporaneous, concise, thorough, organized, confidential); the EHR as an integrated, real-time method of informing the team; records as important evidence in legal matters and the harms of incomplete, inaccurate, untimely, or illegible documentation; the six principles — documentation characteristics (accessible; accurate, relevant, consistent; auditable; clear, concise, complete; legible; thoughtful; timely, contemporaneous, sequential; retrievable), education and training, policies and procedures, protection systems (security and confidentiality), documentation entries (accurate, valid, complete; authenticated with nothing added or inserted; dated and time-stamped; legible; standardized terminology), standardized terminologies; and the honest note that documentation is sometimes viewed as burdensome yet is a necessary and integral aspect of the work of registered nurses. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
